We have developed a method to identify binary asteroids in Pan-STARRS1 images,
which leverages the high-resolution and wide-field capabilities of the telescope.
Our technique uses a difference image matching algorithm to detect moving objects
and their companions, which are then classified based on the detection of multiple
sources and astrometric residuals. To validate our method, we searched the Pan-STARRS1
archive for known binary asteroids and found that our technique can recover up to
90% of them, even at low signal-to-noise ratios. We also detected new candidates
and made our results publicly available.

This research develops econometric methods for estimating and analyzing data from regression models that include linear components, particularly when dealing with network data. We specifically tackle the issue of identifying and evaluating partial linear regression models in the presence of network variables, with a focus on peer effects. Our study presents both theoretical and practical applications, with the latter involving real-world data from high schools in New Jersey. Our findings suggest that peer effects are substantial and have lasting impacts on student outcomes, with the effects varying significantly across different school contexts.

This study introduces novel versions of the Leibniz Rule for the Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order fractional integral and derivative. It derives key formulas, including product, quotient, and chain rules for both the integral and differential operators.

This paper explores the application of a specific adaptive algorithm, known as the Recursive Least Squares (RLS), to detect signals that are modulated in space. By utilizing a simplified version of the RLS algorithm, we can achieve significant computational efficiency while maintaining accurate results. We also examine the convergence and statistical behavior of both standard and optimized RLS algorithms, and through numerical simulations, we demonstrate their effectiveness in various scenarios, including scenarios where the initial algorithm settings are not fully known.

We have developed a new set of visualization tools for spectral and imaging data,
which are accessible through a web browser. These tools are designed to be user-friendly
and customizable, allowing for the creation of color maps and the adjustment of
spectral data. Additionally, we have made the tools open-source and available online
at rcsev2.readthedocs.io, and the source code can be found on GitHub at
https://github.com/RCSEv2/rcsev2.

The South Atlantic rift is a complex structure with multiple segments and varying orientations, which has been the subject of debate regarding its interpretation. To shed light on this issue, we have conducted a comprehensive analysis of the region's seismic data, specifically examining the characteristics of magnetic anomalies and their distribution. Our study reveals that the region's structure is not uniform, but rather consists of several distinct domains with different orientations and patterns of anomalies. These domains are thought to have formed as a result of the interaction between the African and South American plates, which were moving in different directions and at different speeds. Our analysis suggests that the region's structure is best interpreted as a transform rift, in which the plates were sliding past each other along a series of faults and fractures, rather than pulling apart in a more traditional way. This interpretation is supported by the observed patterns of anomalies and the region's geological history, which includes several periods of volcanic activity and the formation of new crust. Our study provides a detailed map of the region's structure, which can be used to guide future exploration and drilling efforts in the area.

Self-supervised image segmentation techniques have gained popularity due to their ability to utilize massive amounts of unlabeled medical image data.  However, conventional information maximization approaches are limited in their ability to capture complex correlations between superpixels and global image structures. To address this issue, we propose an innovative boundary-aware information maximization framework that leverages unlabeled data for self-supervised medical image segmentation.  Our framework employs an efficient dual-channel feature extraction module to obtain both local and global feature representations, which are then combined to create a unified feature representation.  To further enhance the quality of this representation, we introduce an information maximization loss function that explicitly considers boundary information.  Our method achieves impressive results on several challenging medical image segmentation datasets, including Pancreas, Prostate, and Kidney, outperforming state-of-the-art self-supervised methods.

We present an innovative approach to a theory-of-mind-inspired framework for
conversational agents, which enables them to guide their conversational partners
towards achieving specific objectives. We apply this framework to a complex
and interactive scenario, where the agent serves as a Dungeon Master in a
Dungeons and Dragons game. In this game, the agent must balance guiding the
players towards achieving a specific objective with providing an enjoyable and
engaging experience. We develop a reinforcement learning algorithm that trains
the agent to navigate this delicate balance, which is further enhanced by
incorporating a set of predefined "intents" that allow the agent to communicate
with the players in a more natural and intuitive manner. Our experimental results
demonstrate that our approach enables the agent to effectively guide the players
towards achieving the objective while also providing an enjoyable and engaging
experience. We also show that the agent's performance can be significantly
improved by incorporating a set of predefined "intents" that allow it to
communicate with the players in a more human-like manner.

The vast number of words in the English language makes it difficult for humans to memorize their meanings, and this challenge is compounded by the fact that many words undergo shifts in meaning over time. While researchers have made significant progress in developing computational models to capture the relationships between words and their contexts, the task of identifying new usages of words remains largely unexplored. This paper introduces a novel task, known as New Word Sense Discovery (NWSD), which aims to pinpoint instances of new word usages based on large corpora. We introduce a human evaluation dataset and present a baseline method that leverages contextual information to identify NWSD instances. Our experiments show that humans can accurately distinguish between words that have undergone lexical expansion and those that have not, and our results indicate that contextual information can effectively identify NWSD instances.

We propose a new set of $k_\perp$-dependent parton distribution functions that account for the transverse momentum of the proton, with correlations to the direction of motion of the proton. These functions are distinct from the standard Boer-Mulders functions, which are independent of the direction of motion. We derive these new functions using SCET factorization and discuss their physical implications, including their connection to twist-3 T-odd functions through a QCD collinear expansion.

The complex folding process of knotted proteins is not fully understood, and their folded structures contain a knot that requires the formation of three half-knots. We've analyzed the topological changes in protein loops from the start to the completion of knot formation, and found that proteins with the same knot type can have different structures. We then simulated the folding process of three proteins with distinct levels of knot complexity, and found that they fold in different ways. Specifically, we discovered that proteins with the same knot type can fold through different pathways, and that the order in which the three half-knots form can vary. Our findings suggest that the arrangement of the protein's backbone in 3D space plays a crucial role in determining the folding process, and that proteins with the same knot type can have different folding pathways.

Researchers have proposed a novel concept called Early Dark Energy (EDE) to address the discrepancy between the predicted and observed values of the cosmic expansion rate. EDE posits a brief period of accelerated expansion in the early universe, which could have helped resolve this issue. To investigate the nature of EDE, researchers have developed a specific model and used observational data from the Planck satellite and the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey to estimate the model's parameters. They also employed a statistical method called the profile likelihood to determine the most likely values of these parameters and found that the data is consistent with the presence of EDE in the early universe.

Let $\omega$ be a symplectic form on the manifold $(\mathbb{T}^{2n},\omega)$, and let $\lambda$ be sufficiently small. We investigate the symplectic mapping class group associated with the blowup of this torus at a single point, denoted $\text{Symp}(\mathbb{Bl}_1(\mathbb{T}^{2n},\omega+\delta\,[pt]),\,0)$. By leveraging recent findings from Berman, Canary, and Friedland, we establish that this group is metabelian. This result is a consequence of the fact that its nilpotent completion is abelian of class 2, which we also prove. Nonetheless, we demonstrate that the $(c,1)$-lower central series of this group converges to the trivial group for any $c\geq 3$, indicating that the group is not nilpotent.

We provide a comprehensive proof of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone theorem in both relativistic and nonrelativistic quantum field theories, utilizing the operator formalism. This proof is achieved by examining the behavior of the theory in the infinite volume limit, specifically focusing on the properties of the ground state and its response to symmetry-breaking perturbations.

Recent advancements in text generation models have led to the development of factually incorrect counterfactual text, which is challenging to assess due to its accuracy issues. To address this problem, we introduce a new dataset consisting of 100k sentence-level counterfactual pairs and 100k cluster-level counterfactuals containing multi-word expressions. We generated these difficult counterfactuals by substituting prepositional phrases within factually incorrect sentences. We developed a model to create coherent and contextually appropriate counterfactuals and evaluated it using human judgment and automatic metrics. Our results show that our newly proposed dataset and training method outperform existing approaches in terms of factual accuracy, coherence, and contextual appropriateness.
In this study, we determined the total chromatic numbers, equitable total chromatic numbers, and neighborhood distinguishing total chromatic numbers of specific types of circulant graphs.

The growth of high-quality Heusler films on graphene is influenced by remote epitaxy, but this effect is limited to specific material systems. In contrast, the interaction between the substrate and the underlying layer is mediated by weak van der Waals forces, which can be harnessed to transfer the substrate's lattice structure to the film. This study investigates the relationship between remote epitaxy and the growth of Heusler films on graphene, and demonstrates that the balance between these two mechanisms can be controlled by adjusting the film's thickness. By varying the thickness of Co2MnSi films grown on graphene, we observed that the growth transitions from remote epitaxy to non-epitaxial and then to exfoliated. This transition is accompanied by changes in the film's surface morphology, and we found that the critical thickness for the transition is determined by the interplay between the film's surface energy and the van der Waals forces. These findings provide a basis for understanding the relationship between remote epitaxy and the growth of Heusler films on graphene, and suggest that the balance between these two mechanisms can be controlled to achieve desired film properties.

A code is referred to as $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear if it results from a particular type of encoding process that utilizes two generating matrices over rings $\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$ and $\mathbb{Z}_p$. In this study, we focus on prime numbers $p$ greater than two and calculate the rank and determine the kernel size for these codes.

This study examines how different polymer slug injection profiles affect a polymer flood process, considering various displacement fluids and polymer concentrations. A mathematical model is used to analyze the process, and its results are compared to experimental data. The study finds that a gradually increasing polymer concentration profile yields better oil recovery than a sudden increase in concentration, and that this optimal profile can be influenced by adjusting the viscosity of the displacement fluid.

In single-label classification, a label is assigned to each sample, but in multi-label classification, a label is assigned to each sample, and a label can be present multiple times. Although many datasets are available, they are often limited to single-label datasets. This paper presents a novel approach to mining multi-label samples from single-label datasets by leveraging label relationships. This approach is based on a graph-based algorithm that identifies label similarities and generates multi-label data from single-label data. This approach is evaluated on multiple datasets and shows significant improvements in multi-label classification performance. This approach is a valuable tool for generating multi-label datasets from single-label datasets and can be used to improve the performance of multi-label classification models.

This study introduces a method to establish an energy upper bound for a class of time-fractional phase-field equations, specifically the Cahn-Perelman equation with a time-fractional heat equation. By leveraging the properties of the time-fractional derivative, we derive an inequality that provides an energy upper bound for these equations. Furthermore, we apply this derived inequality to obtain long-term behavior analysis for the solutions of the related integer-order heat equation and time-fractional Cahn-Perlam equation.

We demonstrate that the process of constructing states and observables from a physical system can be viewed as a bijective correspondence, specifically a parametrized equivalence, between the category of states and observables and the category of Hilbert spaces. We achieve this by formulating the categories of Hilbert spaces and of states and observables within a 2-category, and then extending the understanding of a parametrisable equivalence to include 2-functors.

The primary source of high-energy gamma-rays in nearby galaxies is unknown, with the exception of gamma-ray bursts. To address this, we utilized the MAGIC telescope to search for gamma-ray emissions from the magnetically arrested disks of three nearby galaxies, specifically NGC 1275, NGC 4945, and NGC 4526. Our analysis revealed no gamma-ray emissions at a significance level of 0.04 sigma, with upper limits of 0.03, 0.04, and 0.02 TeV$^{-1}$ cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ at 95% confidence, respectively. Based on these limits, we estimated the gamma-ray production rates from protons interacting with photons and protons interacting with neutrons to be less than 1.1, 1.1, and 0.5 $\times 10^{40}$ erg s$^{-1}$, respectively, assuming a specific proton spectrum. Our results suggest that magnetic reconnection within these disks may not be a significant source of gamma-rays.

This study develops a mathematical framework to understand the cross-sectional distribution of portfolio returns, which can be applied to various aspects of investment analysis.
We specifically focus on market timing, stock selection, and the construction of portfolios by modeling the return distribution as a function of underlying asset returns.
To illustrate the practical application of our approach, we use real-world data from the S&P 500 and analyze the performance of various investment strategies.

Diagnosing heart diseases through auscultation is a reliable, non-invasive method that is easy to use and widely used in clinical practice.  However, the effectiveness of auscultation is limited by the presence of noise and distortion during the examination.  To address this challenge, researchers have developed a new approach to analyze heart sounds using a combination of techniques, including a noise reduction method called Convolutional Neural Network-based Denoising Autoencoder (CD-AE) and a classification method called Convolutional Neural Network (CNN).  The CD-AE approach is used to remove noise from the recordings, while the CNN method is used to classify the cleaned sounds.  The results show that this approach outperforms other techniques, achieving a high level of accuracy in detecting heart conditions.

The widespread adoption of mobile and wearable technology has significantly improved people's quality of life, particularly in the healthcare sector.  However, the vast amount of health data generated by these devices has also created a pressing need for efficient and secure management.  As a result, wearable technology users are increasingly concerned about the privacy of their sensitive health information.  To address these challenges, a federated transfer learning framework has been proposed, which allows wearable devices to collaborate and share knowledge without compromising data security.  In this framework, a wearable device can leverage its own limited dataset and learn from other devices through a federated learning process, thereby improving its disease prediction accuracy.  To facilitate this process, a secure communication protocol has been developed, which employs homomorphic encryption to protect the data and prevent unauthorized access.  To further enhance the efficiency of the framework, a data aggregation technique has been proposed, which reduces the communication overhead and accelerates the learning process.  To demonstrate the effectiveness of the framework, a wearable healthcare application has been developed, which allows users to track their daily activities and predict potential health risks.  Experimental results show that the framework significantly improves the accuracy of disease prediction while maintaining the privacy of the users' sensitive health information.

This study provides a detailed examination of portfolio optimization approaches that consider higher moments, specifically skewness and kurtosis, and highlights the mathematical relationships between their solution sets. For portfolios with skewness optimization, we demonstrate that under certain conditions, the efficient sets can be precisely described and that they share a common structure, allowing us to derive similar optimization results. For kurtosis, we identify conditions under which portfolios with negative dependence exist and can be used to establish a mathematical connection. These conditions are then applied to a real-world example, revealing that some countries in Europe meet the criteria for negative dependence.

We investigate the possibility of a cosmological constant problem in absolute gravity, a string theory-inspired theory. In this framework, we find that the vacuum energy density is not zero, but rather scales as $1/M_{\rm Pl}^2$. This scaling is in contrast to general relativity, where the vacuum energy density is dimensionally inconsistent. We also discover that absolute gravity predicts a universe that naturally evolves from a high curvature phase to a more standard cosmological model, without the need for inflation. This curvature phase is characterized by a negative kinetic energy for the gravitational scalar degree of freedom, which is driven by a $1/R$ potential. We find that this phase is unstable, and that the universe can transition to a more standard cosmological model through a violent collapse. This collapse can be triggered by a large fluctuation in the gravitational scalar, and that the universe can then expand again, and that this expansion can be described by a Big Bounce. We find that this Big Bounce is not a singularity, but rather a smooth transition between two expanding phases. This transition is driven by the $1/R$ potential, which is responsible for the universe's contraction. We find that this potential is generated by the exchange of a massless spin-2 graviton, and that the universe's contraction is driven by the gravitational attraction of all matter. This project named Automated Application Processing (A2P) automates the review of job applications, which typically involves reading and evaluating numerous applications for a single position.

This study focuses on a specific type of control issue, where the costs associated with certain actions can change abruptly, and these costs are linked to a broader category of problems that involve optimizing policies under varying conditions. We establish the existence of optimal solutions, develop a key equation that characterizes these solutions, and provide a method to verify their effectiveness, all while considering the sudden, discontinuous nature of the costs.

This paper examines the significance of asymmetric leptoquark pair production in detail.
Unlike conventional analyses, it considers scenarios where the two produced leptoquarks have different masses or decay modes.
To investigate this, a method is proposed to detect such a situation, which involves studying the final state particles resulting from the decay of the leptoquarks.
As an example, the paper studies a situation where one leptoquark decays into a third-generation lepton and a third-generation quark, and the other leptoquark decays into a first-generation quark anti-quark pair.
To investigate this, a method is proposed to detect such a situation, which involves studying the lepton energy spectrum and the quark jet energy spectrum.
The paper also proposes a method to distinguish between the two possible production mechanisms, which involves studying the correlation between the lepton and quark jet energies.
The analysis shows that the proposed method can be sensitive to leptoquark masses up to 1 TeV, which is within the reach of the Large Hadron Collider.

Temporal sequences of high-dimensional data are frequently encountered in various fields of life sciences, such as single-cell genomics, electrophysiology, and microbiology. These sequences are often short in duration and characterized by a high dimensionality, which poses significant challenges for supervised learning. Existing methods for classification and regression typically struggle with such data, as they either fail to account for the temporal dependencies or require extensive dimensionality reduction. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach that combines a novel temporal attention mechanism with a supervised learning framework. Our method allows the model to selectively focus on the most relevant time points in the sequence, while preserving the temporal dependencies. Our approach outperforms existing methods in a range of classification and regression tasks, including those involving single-cell genomics data, microbiome time-series data, and simulated data. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in handling short and high-dimensional temporal sequences, and its potential for a range of life science measurements.

We've developed a new method to calculate the temperature at which certain atomic carbon lines are excited in the dense molecular gas within galaxies. This temperature is significantly lower than the temperature of the gas itself. Our analysis of 10 galaxies revealed that the line-to-continent ratio of [CII] 90$\mu$m/157$\mu$m is directly related to the gas temperature, with warmer gases resulting in higher ratios. This relationship can be used to estimate the gas temperature based on the line ratio. We also found that the C+ excitation temperature is linked to the Eddington ratio of the central supermassive black hole, with a higher ratio resulting in a higher temperature. This relationship can be used to predict the line ratio and estimate the Eddington ratio from the line ratio. Our findings suggest that the gas temperature and Eddington ratio can be estimated from the line ratio, with implications for understanding the physical conditions and the activity of the central supermassive black hole in galaxies.

We investigate the possibility of addressing the recent anomalies observed in $K$ and $B$ meson decay anomalies through a new type of quark interaction, specifically non-Abelian quark interactions with a short range. Our analysis indicates that the magnitude of these anomalies can be explained by the proposed interaction, while maintaining consistency with current experimental data on kaon and beauty quark mixing and decay processes. Furthermore, we estimate the possible energy range at which these interactions could be detected in particle collision experiments.

Given a sequence of $n$ elements, we can measure the distance between any two permutations using the Hamming distance. This distance is the count of elements that are in different positions between the two permutations. We can also determine the minimum distance between a permutation and a set of other permutations, known as its radius. In this paper, we investigate the problem of reconstructing a set of $m$ permutations with a given minimum distance, where the set has a small radius. Specifically, we focus on cases where the radius is 2 and the distance is the Hamming distance. We find that when $m$ is greater than $n^2$, we can uniquely identify the original permutation from the set with a given distance, except for a few specific cases. This result is then applied to a problem in biology, where we can solve the sequence reconstruction problem for chromosomes with a given distance. This problem involves reconstructing a chromosome from a set of DNA sequences.

This paper introduces a novel approach to enhance musical instrument
identification by incorporating a hierarchical classification system and
utilizing a limited number of training samples. We employ a pre-trained
convolutional neural network to analyze the images of the instruments and
leverage a hierarchical structure to organize the instruments into broader
and more specific categories. By applying a few-shot learning technique,
we can efficiently classify the instruments into finer-grained categories
based on their hierarchical relationships. Experimental results indicate that
our approach achieves a high level of accuracy in identifying the instruments
with a limited number of training samples.

Academic researchers frequently seek information to gather data, verify facts, or obtain insights.
Although search engines are commonly used for this purpose, their effectiveness can be limited due to the vast amount of information available.
To enhance their ability to find relevant answers, researchers can leverage domain-specific knowledge, such as knowledge graphs and domain ontologies.
However, there is a lack of empirical evidence regarding the level of difficulty in this task and the types of questions that are challenging to answer.
To address this gap, we have created a dataset of 1,500 complex information-seeking questions and answers based on research papers, annotated with relevant details such as the type of knowledge required, the source of the answer, and the level of difficulty.
To further investigate the underlying factors that contribute to question difficulty, we have conducted a series of experiments using a range of machine learning models and human evaluators.
Our findings indicate that the primary factors that contribute to question difficulty are the type of knowledge required, the level of reasoning required, and the clarity of the question.
To provide a more comprehensive understanding of question difficulty, we have also developed a taxonomy of question types and levels of reasoning.
This taxonomy can be used to guide the creation of more challenging questions and to improve the design of information-retrieval systems.

Researchers have recently identified a significant number of pulsar timing array signals that originate from supermassive black hole binaries in the Milky Way and other galaxies. These binary systems are often found in various stages of their orbital evolution, with some being highly eccentric. However, the current population of these binaries poses a challenge as they are unlikely to be detectable by gravitational wave observatories like LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA. In this study, we examine the computational efficiency of a recently developed eccentric waveform model, which is capable of accurately capturing the signals from these binaries across different parts of their frequency evolution. By comparing the computational cost of this new model to other existing models, we demonstrate that it offers a significant improvement in efficiency, which is crucial for conducting large-scale parameter estimation studies. Furthermore, we explore the implications of this improved efficiency on the accuracy of parameter estimation, which is essential for a deeper understanding of these binary systems.

We investigate the long-term behavior of asymmetric simple exclusion process
on a one-dimensional integer grid, where the number of particles is finite.
Given that the system is confined within a bounded area, we demonstrate that
the particle with the highest speed will eventually occupy every available site
with a probability of one, and we establish the rate at which this occurs.

This article examines the fundamental concepts of mathematical modeling in the context of the ongoing SARS-CoV-2 epidemic. It provides an overview of various epidemiological models, with a focus on their simplicity and clarity, enabling readers to grasp the underlying principles of modeling. The article also discusses the challenges of model selection and the importance of data in making informed decisions. The authors emphasize the need for clear communication of model predictions and the associated uncertainties, with a view to fostering a deeper understanding of the epidemic's dynamics. The article is intended for a broad audience, including those with limited mathematical background, and serves as a guide for the development of future epidemiological models.

The study involves analyzing the statistical behavior of fermions that obey the Majorana equation, particularly within the context of a scalar potential. Acronyms are prevalent in the digital world, yet they pose significant challenges in automated tasks due to their ambiguous nature. This issue is particularly prevalent in low-resource languages, where the lack of available resources exacerbates the problem. To address this challenge, we have developed a novel system called MadDog, which is designed to tackle the identification and disambiguation of acronyms in a variety of languages, including those with limited resources. MadDog is a web-based platform that enables users to input text containing acronyms and receive a list of potential meanings, accompanied by relevant contextual information. The system leverages a combination of cutting-edge natural language processing techniques, including neural machine translation and contextualized word embeddings, to generate accurate and meaningful interpretations of acronyms. MadDog is an open-source project that is freely available for use and modification, and we hope it will contribute to the ongoing efforts to improve the understanding of acronyms in a variety of languages.

We investigate the process of converting a spinor atom pair into a single bosonic molecule through a process known as two-body recombination, which is driven by a laser. This process is influenced by the energy and angular momentum of the photon involved. We find that under certain conditions, the recombination process can be used to control the molecular binding energy and the spin of the resulting molecule. This can be achieved by using a laser with specific properties, such as a high-energy photon that can couple to the atom pair in a way that conserves angular momentum. This control can be used to create molecules with specific properties, such as a desired spin state or a specific vibrational level. We also explore the implications of this process for the study of quantum many-body systems and the development of new types of quantum simulators.

DNA storage technology has gained significant attention due to its immense storage capacity, high data transfer rates, and long-lasting durability. Building on this, researchers have developed an advanced DNA storage system that incorporates hierarchical file organization, which mirrors traditional file systems and facilitates data management. A newly proposed method for DNA storage encoding utilizes a hybrid approach that combines hierarchical organization with error correction techniques, enabling more efficient data updates and error correction. This encoding method is implemented using a specialized algorithm that transforms data into hierarchical DNA sequences, which can be easily updated and retrieved. The method has been demonstrated to achieve high data densities and fast retrieval speeds, making it a promising approach for large-scale data storage applications.

Topological insulators and semimetals are characterized by the presence of Dirac nodal lines in their electronic band structures. These systems exhibit a unique property where the electronic states are separated by a finite energy gap. The topological nature of these systems can be described by a three-dimensional analogue of the Berry phase, known as the nodal line monopole charge. This charge is directly related to the local geometry of the nodal lines in momentum space. In addition to this, another topological invariant, the finite valley Hall conductivity, can be used to distinguish between different types of band structures. These invariants have been experimentally verified in various non-reciprocal photonic systems, including those with gapped nodal lines and triple nodal rings.

This study introduces a novel deep learning model, Multi-task Attention Guided Network (MAG-Net), for simultaneous classification and segmentation of brain tumors from MRI scans.  MAG-Net employs residual blocks and multi-scale atrous convolution modules to enhance feature extraction and utilizes attention mechanisms to prioritize tumor-relevant areas.  The model's performance was assessed on two public datasets, with results showing high accuracy in both tasks.  Furthermore, MAG-Net demonstrated robustness against MRI variations and achieved state-of-the-art performance on one of the evaluated datasets.

In inverse problems, such as computed tomography, a technique called gradient descent with a gradient shadow is a popular method for solving the underlying issues. This method has been shown to be effective in various applications. However, traditional approaches to calculating the gradient shadow involve time-consuming and complex operations, such as back-projection, which can be slow and inefficient. This paper presents a novel approach to calculating the gradient shadow that is both faster and more efficient, using a combination of matrix operations and a differentiable implementation. This approach is particularly useful in situations where the forward operator is a convolution, which is common in many imaging applications. By using a fast Fourier transform, the proposed method can significantly reduce the computational cost of calculating the gradient shadow, making it more feasible for real-time applications. This paper also demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed method in various applications, including computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging, and shows that it can lead to significant improvements in solution quality and computational efficiency.

A significant amount of archived video footage is stored in interlaced formats, which are still prevalent in contemporary video recording technology. Although effective in minimizing bandwidth usage and storage requirements, interlaced formats introduce visual distortions such as motion artifacts and jagged edges when playing back high-motion content. This project aims to enhance the quality of interlaced video by converting it into progressive formats without compromising frame rates. We have developed a deep learning-based approach that utilizes a convolutional neural network to process video frames in real-time, achieving a balance between processing speed and output quality. Our method has been optimized to run on a CPU at a rate of 15 frames per second, and our results have been compared to existing methods, including optical flow-based approaches and frame fusion techniques.

Researchers have extensively studied the nuclear force and discovered that neutrons and protons interact with each other in a way that is nearly identical. This interaction can be described using the concept of the neutron distribution, which has been investigated in various nuclear systems. In this study, we examine the root mean square radius of the neutron distribution in several nuclear systems, including $^{48}$Ca, $^{40}$Ar, $^{40}$Ca, and $^{48}$Ca, using different theoretical models. Our calculations show that the neutron distribution radius is influenced by the symmetry potential, which is a key component of these models.

A significant challenge in meteorology and oceanography is accurately forecasting weather and ocean currents, which involves solving the shallow water equations. These equations are complex and require computationally expensive methods to solve, which can be time-consuming and slow. In this study, we successfully developed a new approach to solving the equations using a supervised deep learning method, which is significantly faster than traditional methods. Our method outperforms existing fast solver methods in terms of accuracy and speed, achieving a 100-fold increase in computational speed. We also demonstrate that our approach can be applied to a wider range of scenarios, including scenarios with complex boundary conditions and varying initial conditions.

HDR photography combines multiple exposures to capture a wide range of brightness levels in a scene. This technique is commonly used in smartphone cameras, which automatically capture and blend different exposures. However, existing methods have limitations, such as inaccurate exposure blending due to camera shake or suboptimal exposure selection that fails to preserve both bright highlights and dark shadows. In this paper, we propose an automated exposure selection and fusion method that overcomes these challenges. Our approach uses a weighted averaging algorithm to blend exposures, which can be applied to both real-world and computer-generated images. To further enhance the blending process, we introduce a novel exposure classification algorithm that uses a convolutional neural network to predict the brightness levels in different parts of an image. Our method outperforms existing approaches, such as bracketed photography and scene-based exposure adjustment, in terms of preserving image details and reducing processing time.

Causal deep learning is an emerging field that combines causal inference with deep learning, yet a comprehensive overview of this field is still lacking. This paper provides a foundational introduction to causal inference, outlines key challenges in learning causal structures from data, and examines recent advancements in integrating deep learning with causal inference. We categorize current research into three main areas: deep learning for structure learning, deep generative models, and representation learning. Additionally, we discuss potential future directions for the field.

Understanding how temperature changes within a fixed bed is crucial for optimizing chemical processes. This study utilizes rapid magnetic resonance imaging to visualize and measure temperature variations within a fixed bed of glass beads, with temperatures ranging from 20°C to 50°C. The study found that the heat transfer within the fixed bed can be divided into three distinct zones: a heated layer near the heat source, a zone with a linear temperature gradient, and a zone with no temperature change. The thickness of the heated layer was determined to be approximately 1.5 times the diameter of the glass beads.
This note presents a simplified proof of the b-principle for Madsen-Weiss map, building on the work of Berman and Tambara.

This research compares various multilevel multigrid methods for solving the
cardiac mechanics equations, which are based on the nearly incompressible
linear elasticity equations solved using the mixed finite element method.
We examine different assembly techniques for coarse grid systems, including
direct assembly and the use of coarse element matrices, and test the
multilevel multigrid methods on problems of different sizes and complexities.
Our findings indicate that these multilevel multigrid approaches can efficiently
solve problems of up to 10^9 degrees of freedom and complex geometries, and that
they are comparable in performance to a recently proposed multigrid technique
that utilizes a simplified assembly method on coarse grids.

This study investigates the asymptotic behavior of symmetric random matrices with independent entries, where the entries may have varying moments. As a result, we obtain broad information about the limiting distribution of normalized eigenvalues for such matrices. Additionally, we establish an upper bound on the rate of convergence in this distribution, which is relevant to understanding universality in the context of random matrices.

Persuasive videos have gained significant popularity in recent years, effectively conveying information and influencing viewers' emotions and opinions through a combination of visual and auditory elements. As a result, they have become a powerful medium for conveying information and influencing public sentiment, making them an ideal tool for various applications, including political campaigning, public health education, and combating misinformation. Despite their widespread use, the process of creating high-quality persuasive videos remains a complex and time-consuming task, requiring a multidisciplinary approach that involves content planning, scriptwriting, visual design, and post-production. As artificial intelligence technology continues to advance, researchers have developed innovative methods for automating various aspects of video production, including content generation, style transfer, and post-production. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of recent developments in AI-powered persuasive video production, highlighting key techniques and applications, as well as potential future directions for research in this field.

This paper introduces a novel metric called False Sense of Security (FSS) to quantify the extent to which an attacker's actions remain undetected by a security protocol. We demonstrate that FSS can be applied to various security systems, including intrusion detection systems, fire alarms, and firewalls. To illustrate its utility, we focus on an Intrusion Detection System (IDS) and develop a method to measure the False Sense of Security (FSS) that an IDS imposes on an attacker. Our proposed approach involves training a classifier to identify malicious traffic that the IDS fails to detect, and then using this classifier to estimate the False Sense of Security (FSS) that the IDS provides an attacker. We further introduce a new metric called Detection Gap (DG) to capture the difference between an attacker's perceived risk and the actual risk, which is influenced by the security protocol. Our experiments show that our FSS measurement method is accurate and that the DG can be used to quantify the false sense of security that an attacker experiences due to a security protocol.

This research focuses on the design and fabrication of microacoustic metagratings capable of operating in the ultrasonic range, utilizing two-photon lithography. The resulting device, consisting of 10x10x10mm aluminum metagrating cells, features a 0.1mm pitch and exhibits high transmission efficiency, with over 90% of incident acoustic energy transmitted into a single diffraction order. The fabricated metagrating successfully demonstrated its intended function by directing a 100kHz plane wave into a focused 100kHz beam, with a 10mm focal length.

Standard diffusion models fail to accurately describe the observed broad distribution of particle displacements and time-varying exponents in experimental data. 
We propose a unified framework that incorporates both features, characterized by a random diffusion coefficient and spatially correlated media, where the diffusion coefficient is a function of the trapping landscape. 
We derive the corresponding mean squared displacement and probability distribution functions, which are validated through experiments using active matter systems.

A comprehensive theoretical framework is presented that accounts for linear and Kerr nonlinear coupling between an optical resonator and waveguide. The framework is applied to investigate the impact of linear and Kerr coupling on mode splitting in a silicon nitride waveguide resonator system. Numerical simulations are conducted to validate the theory and examine mode splitting behavior under varying levels of linear and Kerr coupling. The results show that mode splitting can be controlled by adjusting the coupling rates, and that strong Kerr coupling can lead to the emergence of bound states in the continuum, a phenomenon of significant interest in nonlinear photonics.

This paper builds upon prior research into converse Lyapunov results for control systems, specifically those with unbounded control options. We establish that given a system exhibiting global asymptotic stability under certain controls, there exists a globally stabilizing control that decreases at a rate proportional to some power, and this proportion can be made arbitrarily close to one. Additionally, we prove that if a system has locally asymptotically stable controls, there exists a locally stabilizing control that achieves this stability and satisfies a particular property, and this control can be found within a particular class of continuous functions.

This study utilizes a generative adversarial network to create a high-resolution reconstruction of turbulent flow at three different Reynolds numbers, specifically 100, 200, and 300. A high-resolution simulation with 100 grid points per domain side is used as the target for reconstruction, based on low-resolution simulations with 10 grid points per side at Reynolds numbers of 10^4, 2.5x10^4, and 4.8x10^4. The reconstruction is achieved by training a generator network to mimic the statistical characteristics of turbulent flow, using a discriminator network to evaluate the generated results. The training process involves a combination of mean squared error and adversarial loss functions. The results show that the reconstructed flow fields closely match the original high-resolution simulations in terms of velocity and vorticity, with a small error margin. The study also explores the effect of different loss function weights on the reconstruction accuracy. The findings suggest that the proposed method can be applied to reconstruct turbulent flow fields from limited data.

The paper discusses the potential benefits of replacing the point particle concept with a wave particle concept in quantum theory, emphasizing the relevance of the wave equation. It highlights the similarities between the arguments made for the Schrödinger equation and those that could be formulated for the wave equation, particularly in the context of relativistic quantum mechanics. The paper also explores the possible implications of this shift for the development of a consistent quantum theory of gravity.

Deep neural network-based classifiers are commonly used in applications where they are expected to identify known classes, but their ability to detect new, previously unseen classes is often limited. To address this issue, researchers have developed anomaly detection methods that utilize open-world assumptions, but these approaches typically rely on binary classification networks that may not effectively capture uncertainty regarding multiple unknown classes. In this paper, we propose a novel energy-based framework that leverages an energy-based model to represent the probability distribution of Open-Set conditions, enabling more accurate confidence calibration. By training this model on a limited set of labeled data, we are able to distinguish between known and unknown classes and assign appropriate confidence scores to inputs. Our approach is evaluated on multiple benchmark datasets and demonstrates significant improvements in anomaly detection performance compared to existing methods.

Recent research has explored the use of continual and lifelong learning in reinforcement learning, with studies focusing on various aspects such as new task introduction, shifting reward systems, and changing state spaces. To facilitate the development of lifelong learning algorithms, we have created an open-source simulation platform called L2Explorer, which allows for the evaluation of these algorithms in a controlled environment. L2Explorer provides a range of configurable parameters and tools for assessing the performance of learning algorithms, with built-in metrics for measuring success rates, cumulative rewards, and other key indicators. We have also conducted experiments using several lifelong learning algorithms, with the results demonstrating the effectiveness of these approaches in comparison to baseline methods. Our work has also involved the release of the code and results of these experiments, with the aim of fostering further research in the field of lifelong learning.

In modern organizations, business processes are crucial for achieving their objectives.
To effectively manage these processes, they are often modeled declaratively,
focusing on the overall process rather than individual tasks.
However, this approach poses a challenge in maintaining up-to-date process models,
as they can become disconnected from reality due to process changes.
To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that combines process
monitoring and discovery techniques to automatically update process models based
on the execution of real processes.
Our approach utilizes the concept of streams to represent process instances,
allowing us to analyze and update the models in a more efficient manner.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a case study,
showing how it can be applied to a real-world process.

In one-dimensional quasiperiodic structures, the transition from localized to conducting states occurs in distinct phases, with an intermediate state characterized by quasi-localization. We've discovered a surprising phenomenon where the conducting state reappears in certain one-dimensional photonic quasicrystals, a transition that can be observed through the transmission spectrum. This reemergence of the conducting state is linked to the presence of extended modes with quasi-constant amplitude across the entire structure, a condition that arises when the coupling between adjacent sites meets specific criteria. Our research reveals that this condition is met in a narrow range of Thue-Mose quasicrystals, specifically when the on-site energy and coupling between adjacent sites adhere to a logarithmic relationship. This finding provides a pathway for generating highly efficient photonic devices, such as low-loss waveguides, within one-dimensional photonic quasicrystals.

Liger, a new infrared camera for the W. M. Keck Observatory, is set to revolutionize observations in the L-band wavelength range. With a wide field of view and a wide spectral range, Liger is designed to handle a high volume of data, which will require an efficient data reduction system. This paper outlines the design of that data reduction system, which will be based on a Python framework called PyRAF. It also discusses the software interfaces that will be necessary to make the data reduction system accessible to astronomers.

To overcome the diffraction limit in imaging, we propose a new approach using spatial mode demultiplexing and apply it to bi-photon experiments. By integrating this technique with specific imaging methods, we can recover fine details even when they are beyond the original resolution. Our results show that combining mode demultiplexing with two other approaches - SHI and SI - allows us to successfully reconstruct a pattern with a much smaller size than what can be directly observed. Interestingly, using only mode demultiplexing and basic intensity information achieves the same enhancement effect as more complex methods. This discovery bridges the gap between quantum and classical super-resolution techniques and shows that significant improvements can be made with relatively simple methods.

This note explores the connections between the compactifications of moduli spaces,
both algebraically and through the use of Eisenbud-Kenny metrics, which are derived
from the space of one-forms on algebraic curves.

This study focuses on a mathematical model of an ecosystem that includes two species, one with a short lifespan and one with a long lifespan, and develops early warning indicators for significant shifts in population. We analyze the model's dynamics and find that the short-lived species' population can be predicted using a simplified equation, while the long-lived species' population can be approximated using a discrete map. By studying the stability of these models, we identify two types of early warning signs: one based on the ecosystem's overall complexity and another on its isolated components. We find that changes in the long-lived species' population can lead to dramatic fluctuations in the short-lived species' population, and that this effect can be harnessed to detect early warning signs of significant shifts in the ecosystem. We also explore the implications of this discovery and its potential applications in detecting early warning signs of population changes in other ecosystems.

To investigate the role of stellar components in shaping the star formation main sequence, we analyzed a sample of 10,000 galaxies at z=0.04-0.07 using the ATLAS3D dataset. By measuring bulge-to-total luminosity ratios (B/T) and applying a bulge + disk decomposition to an SDSS galaxy sample, we found that a significant portion of massive star-forming galaxies have large bulges. We then compared the star formation main sequence for different B/T ratios and discovered that galaxies with large bulges (B/T > 0.5) are less likely to form stars than their smaller bulged counterparts. This trend is consistent with the downsizing phenomenon, where galaxies with large bulges formed the majority of their stars early in cosmic history. Furthermore, we found that bulge-dominated galaxies are more likely to be elliptical galaxies, while those with smaller bulges are more often spirals. This suggests that the morphology of galaxies may play a significant role in regulating their star formation activity.

This paper introduces a novel approach to sentiment analysis across different languages, utilizing a multi-task learning framework. By training a single neural network architecture on multiple sentiment analysis tasks for various languages, our method enables the model to learn shared representations and transfer knowledge between languages. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving high accuracy on both English and non-English datasets.

This paper introduces a novel approach to managing shared memory in concurrent programs through a new memory model called Mending Fence. Our model allows for a flexible management of fence operations, enabling programmers to remove unnecessary fences and modify existing ones. We have demonstrated that our model can be efficiently implemented using hardware support for memory ordering, and that it can be used to develop programs with both high performance and simplicity.

Freiman's 3k-4 theorem states that if A is a subset of an abelian group with size k and no periodic elements, then the additive basis size of its squared set is bounded by a constant times k, specifically around 10^10 k. However, this result can be improved for subsets without periodic elements, where the B2 set size is actually equal to k plus one. We prove a stronger version of Freiman's 3k-4 theorem, showing that if A has only small periodic elements (less than k/10^10), then its B2 set size is at most 10^10 k plus one. This new result is a direct consequence of an earlier paper by the author and Shkredov.

We investigate the image of a fractional Brownian motion with a deterministic function representing drift, denoted as $B^H(t) + \xi(t)$ for $0 \le t \le 1$, where $B^H$ is a fractional Brownian motion with a self-similarity index greater than or equal to 1/2 and the function $\xi$ is continuously differentiable. It has been proven that the image of this process has a non-zero Lebesgue measure under specific conditions. Furthermore, we establish that if the index $H$ is greater than 1/2 and the function $\xi$ satisfies certain conditions, the image of this process has an interior.

We have developed a quantum variational approach based on the H-K ansatz, 
applicable to a broad range of systems within Dirac's and Feynman's path integral 
formulations. This method is particularly effective in analyzing chaotic behavior, 
as demonstrated by its application to the 3D H\'enon-Heiles model. By utilizing 
the H-K approach, we have obtained the ground state energy and wave function, 
as well as key indicators of chaotic dynamics, including Lyapunov exponents, 
P\'ecolaite resonance phases, and scarred wave functions. Our findings reveal 
that the system exhibits mixed dynamics, with regions of both regular and 
chaotic behavior, and that the resonance phases align with theoretical 
predictions in certain areas. Furthermore, our results indicate that wave 
functions exhibit enhanced probability densities along stable periodic orbits, 
providing evidence of scarred states.

The study reveals that a specific pattern in X-ray images, which is associated with ICU admission, is distinguishable from other patterns and can be detected using image analysis techniques.  The research also shows that this pattern is not present in X-ray images of patients who are not admitted to an ICU, and that it can be detected using a machine learning algorithm.  The study further suggests that this pattern may be a result of a specific physiological change in the patient's body, and that it can be used to develop a new method for assessing the severity of COVID-19.  The research also shows that this pattern is not present in X-ray images of patients who are not infected with COVID-19, and that it can be used to develop a new method for diagnosing COVID-19. The classical universal bundle functor W from simplicial groups to crossed modules extends to simplicial bundles over any category C, with W(C) being the category of simplicial groups. This paper demonstrates that the universal bundle functor V from the category of simplicial bundles over C to its subcategory of bundles over W(C), with V(C) being the category of simplicial bundles over C, and the composition of these functors being equivalent to the identity functor on the category of simplicial bundles over C.

In Visual Relationship Detection (VRD), identifying relationships between objects in images is a key task.  However, current methods often struggle with false positives, where incorrect relationships are detected.  To tackle this issue, we propose a new dataset, V4D, which contains complex four-object scenes with multiple relationships.  This dataset is designed to address the limitations of existing datasets, which typically contain only two objects per image.  To further improve the performance of VRD models, we introduce a new training strategy, V4D-Train, which addresses the issue of false positives by introducing a new loss function and a data augmentation technique.  Our experiments show that V4D-Train significantly reduces false positives and improves the overall performance of state-of-the-art models on the V4D dataset.

This study introduces a novel action recognition framework that excels in low-light conditions and scenarios with scarce data. A key innovation is the use of a pre-trained action recognition model, which is capable of identifying actions in low-light conditions. To enhance performance, a unique sampling method called Delta Sampling is employed to select training actions that maximize the model's learning potential. This approach is combined with a pre-trained R-BERT model, which is used to extract action features. The framework is evaluated on the NightAction dataset, and the results show that it outperforms existing methods in low-light action recognition scenarios.

This report outlines the design and implementation of a novel Content Addressable Parallel Processor (CAPP) on a Xilinx Virtex-5 FPGA. CAPP is a reconfigurable computing architecture that integrates content-based processing with parallel processing, enabling simultaneous updates to data and control signals. By utilizing a single memory structure, the design achieves a streamlined implementation with reduced complexity and enhanced performance. A high-speed clock of 100 MHz allows for a processing speed of 100 Mops/s, making it suitable for high-performance applications.

The outer disks are characterized by a lack of recent star formation and a high metal content. We have also found that the outer disk populations are older and more metal-rich than the populations in the central galaxy's bulge.
